reasoning: English loanword 'dozen' adapted to Arabic vowels, giving darzan. The vowels are my best judgement, since the word has no fixed spelling norm. دستة (dasta) is also heard for a dozen or set.
ق is a glottal stop in everyday urban speech. Taa marbuta after ر is a. The word also means a section, item or segment of a show, but paragraph is correct.
Long aa in the second syllable. Taa marbuta after م is e. Covers both pigeon and dove.
The article assimilates to د: id-daktoor. 3ind is the usual Palestinian 'at / with'. The vowels of maw3id and daktoor vary slightly between speakers.
Literally 'it has no need', said as 'there's no need / no point'. Palestinian ilu (short u) and verbless ma negation. The و in the spelling is only a spelling device: the vowel is short.

Emphatic ظ is written TH. The Levantine verb takes the fi3il shape (THihir). It is understood and used, but everyday speech often prefers بان (baan) for 'appeared' and طلع (Tili3) or إجا (ija) for 'showed up'.
Medial hamza is written '. Taa marbuta after ف is e. 'rel. branch' is too terse: it means a religious sect, denomination or community, such as a Christian denomination or the Druze.
Urban Palestinian says ث as t in native words, as in تَالِت for third. So ثامن is taamin, not thaamin.
Levantine fi3il adjective shape, 3ifin. Means moldy, rotten or putrid, and is also used for anything foul.
Everyday Palestinian 'let's start': khalliina plus a subjunctive. I read نبلش as the form II verb ballash, so nballish. Everything is colloquial.
Hamza after the article is written: il-'arjantiina. The spelling with final ا follows the entry; the more standard form is الأرجنتين. Country name, said the same in Palestinian speech.
Long oo in yoom. Taa marbuta after ع is a. Palestinian jum3a, with short u.
Country name following the MSA shape with the final -iya reduced to -ya. The vowel quality of the first syllable (uu) is a judgement call.
Initial vowel is a short i. ط is emphatic, so T. The ي in the spelling is not a long vowel in speech, so I respelled it as إِطَالْيَا.
Taa marbuta after ي is e. Common idiom for 'barely / with great effort', e.g. bil-3aafye wiSilt. It can also mean 'by force'.
ض is emphatic, so D. Word-initial hamza is only a vowel seat. Also means land or earth, and 3al-arD is 'on the floor'.
Levantine fa3laan from a hollow root keeps the diphthong: jaw3aan. The alternative jуu3aan is less typical of Palestinian speech.
An academic, MSA-borrowed word, so I keep ق as q. Some urban speakers glottalise it as manTi'. Also means reasoning or way of thinking.
Palestinian shughul with short u in both syllables; some speakers say shighil. Means work or job, and also 'stuff / business'.
mish negates adjectives. ط is emphatic, so T. In slang it can also mean 'unbelievable / crazy'.
Taa marbuta after ل is e. The word is understood, but Palestinians more often say هزة أرضية (hazze arDiyye) or زلزال (zilzaal) for an earthquake.
7akeet is the 1st-person past of 7aka, with ee before the clitic -lu. ع plus the article assimilates before ت: 3at-tilifoon. The vowels of tilifoon vary slightly between speakers.
In the construct phrase, kura becomes kurat. سلة is salle with a doubled l. Often said with the article, kurat is-salle.
Taa marbuta after س is e. MSA-origin word used normally in Palestinian conversation. Also means 'policy'.
Loanword from French ascenseur, used in everyday speech instead of the formal MSA مصعد. The vowel quality of the final syllable varies a little between speakers.
